the STI/HIV testing-&-treatment node (Thread F · SRH). "Owning your sexual health: testing is power, not
shame." 84 researched, India-grounded, comprehensive-but-never-explicit scenarios across the know-your-status
→ prevention-stack → talk-about-it → treat-and-thrive → dignity-no-stigma → own-it-decide arc, each encoded
as one of the shared v2 play actions (strike-rewrite / branch / reflect / sort / match / role-play / spot)
no binary "tap the right card". Lead: strike-rewrite (bust the myth ×18), branch (own it ×18), sort (fact vs
myth ×13). Testing is self-care not shame; build a prevention stack; talk to a partner; TREATMENT WORKS (HIV
manageable, U=U undetectable=untransmittable; most STIs treatable, several curable); DIGNITY for all, zero

distress to help. Builds on g23 (Outbreak); pairs g29; links g31 (Mutual). Rendered by the shared engine
title: Status: Know It
greet: Hey, it’s Lensy. 🩺 Testing is self-care, not shame. Build your prevention stack, know treatment works, and stand for dignity: zero stigma.

badge.title: Status: Know It! 🩺
badge.blurb: You know testing is power not shame, can build a prevention stack and talk to a partner, know treatment works (U=U), and stand for dignity with zero stigma. 💛

helpLine: Free HIV/STI testing: find a NACO ICTC centre or ask a doctor, who will explain what stays private. If anyone pressures or exploits you, call Childline 1098.
reassure: Testing is power, not shame: an STI or HIV is a health matter, never a verdict; with treatment people live full lives (U=U). If pressured, call Childline 1098.

scenarios.hook: "Getting tested means you did something wrong."

myth.un: Getting tested means you did something wrong.
myth.re: Testing is routine, responsible self-care, like any other health check.
myth.why: Knowing your status is how you look after yourself and others.

scenarios.relearn: Testing is smart self-care, not an admission of guilt.

scenarios.hook: "Only certain kinds of people need to get tested."

myth.un: Only certain kinds of people need testing.
myth.re: Testing is about behaviour, not identity; anyone sexually active can benefit.
myth.why: Linking it to 'types of people' is stigma, not science.

scenarios.relearn: Testing is about behaviour, not identity; it's for anyone active.

scenarios.hook: "You can tell if someone has an STI just by looking."

myth.un: You can tell someone's status by looking at them.
myth.re: Many STIs have no visible signs; only testing tells you.
myth.why: Looks reveal nothing; a test reveals the facts.

scenarios.relearn: You can't tell status by looking; only a test tells you.

scenarios.hook: "Home or self-tests aren't reliable."

myth.un: Self-tests aren't reliable.
myth.re: Self-tests are reliable when used correctly and read after the window period.
myth.why: They're a valid, private way to know your status.

scenarios.relearn: Self-tests are reliable when used right and read after the window period.

It puts you in charge of your health

scenarios.relearn: Acting, protecting and taking charge are smart; 'dirty', 'those people' and 'branded' are stigma.

scenarios.relearn: Windows, free confidential care and valid self-tests are true; 'one forever', symptom-only and 'tell by looking' are myths.

scenarios.hook: You've recently become sexually active, and testing crosses your mind.

steps.prompt: Nothing feels wrong with your body. What do you do about testing?

options.text: Wait until something feels wrong before testing
options.then: Weeks pass with no signs, and testing slips off your mind.

options.text: Test once now, and never think about it again
options.then: You decide one test will settle it for good, and plan nothing after that.

options.text: Make testing a regular part of your health routine
options.then: You set a reminder. Testing starts to feel like any other check-up.

options.text: Ask your partner if they think you need to
options.then: Your partner shrugs. "We seem fine." The question goes nowhere.

steps.why: Many STIs have no symptoms, so regular testing is how you actually know.

steps.prompt: You're not sure where someone your age can actually get tested. What do you do?

options.text: Ask in the class group chat where people go
options.then: Three people reply with jokes, and one asks why you want to know.

options.text: Ask your school counsellor or a doctor where to go
options.then: The counsellor names a youth-friendly clinic and says it's confidential.

options.text: Order the cheapest test you can find online
options.then: A packet arrives with unclear instructions and a brand you can't check.

options.text: Wait until you're 18 and can go on your own
options.then: Months stretch ahead with no answers about your health.

steps.why: A counsellor or doctor can point you to confidential, youth-friendly care.

steps.prompt: Months later, a clinic poster reminds you about regular testing. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since you feel completely fine
options.then: Feeling fine becomes your only check, and it can't tell you much.

options.text: Tell yourself you'll go when life is less busy
options.then: Exams come and go, and the poster fades from memory.

options.text: Test only if a partner asks you to
options.then: Nobody asks, so you never go.

options.text: Book a test, like any routine check-up
options.then: The visit is quick, and you set your next reminder on the way out.

steps.why: Feeling fine says little. Testing regularly is how you stay up to date.

scenarios.debrief: Routine testing, not symptom-waiting, is how you own your health.
scenarios.relearn: Make testing routine; don't wait for symptoms.

scenarios.hook: You want an HIV test, but you live in a small town where everyone knows everyone.

steps.prompt: You're scared someone will see you or find out. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since everyone will find out anyway
options.then: The worry stays, and so does not knowing.

options.text: Travel to a big city where nobody could recognise you
options.then: The trip would take a whole day and a story for your parents, so you put it off.

options.text: Find a NACO ICTC centre, where testing is confidential
options.then: The centre is a short bus ride away, and the poster says free and confidential.

options.text: Use a fake name at the nearest private lab
options.then: The lab asks for ID, and you leave flustered.

steps.why: ICTC testing is free and confidential, so privacy is built into the service.

steps.prompt: You'd feel braver with someone along. Who do you ask?

options.text: A classmate who's fun but talks a lot
options.then: She agrees, and mentions it to two people by lunch.

options.text: An adult you trust, like your aunt or school counsellor
options.then: Your aunt says yes at once and asks nothing you don't want to share.

options.text: Your best friend, who thinks testing is a fuss
options.then: She comes along but sighs all the way, and you nearly turn back.

options.text: Your younger cousin, who won't understand anyway
options.then: He gets bored and asks loudly what you're there for.

steps.why: A trusted adult can support you through it and keep it private.

steps.prompt: When you go for the test, the counsellor asks about your worries first. What do you do?

options.text: Give vague answers so nothing can be traced
options.then: She can't tailor her advice, and you leave with questions.

options.text: Ask her to promise in writing she'll tell no one
options.then: She smiles and explains that confidentiality is already the rule there.

options.text: Answer honestly, knowing it stays confidential
options.then: She listens and explains each step. Your shoulders drop.

options.text: Ask to skip the questions and just do the test
options.then: She explains the chat helps, but you rush through it anyway.

steps.why: ICTC counselling is confidential, so honesty gets you the right care.

scenarios.debrief: Free, confidential testing exists; privacy is part of the service.
scenarios.relearn: NACO ICTC offers free, confidential testing.

scenarios.hook: A week after a condom broke, a rapid test at a clinic comes back negative.

steps.prompt: The test was quick, and the result looks clear. What do you do?

options.text: Treat the negative as the final word and relax
options.then: You relax, not knowing the test may have been too early.

options.text: Go to another lab tomorrow for a second opinion
options.then: Tomorrow's test is just as early, and says the same thing.

options.text: Ask the counsellor when you should test again
options.then: She explains the window period and books you in for a re-test.

options.text: Ask your partner to test instead, to settle it
options.then: Your partner tests, but their result can't stand in for your own re-test.

steps.why: A test too soon after exposure can miss an infection. The window period matters.

steps.prompt: Over the next few days, your mind keeps going back to it. What do you do?

options.text: Test again every few days to check
options.then: Every early result says the same, and none of them settles the worry.

options.text: Talk it through with an adult you trust
options.then: Your aunt listens, then helps you work out when to test again.

options.text: Read worst-case stories online at night
options.then: The stories get scarier, and sleep gets harder.

options.text: Decide one negative is enough, and skip the re-test
options.then: The worry fades, but the question is never really answered.

steps.why: Sharing the wait with someone you trust makes it easier to see it through.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, the clinic sends a reminder that a follow-up test is due. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since the first test was negative
options.then: The first result stays your only answer, though it came too soon.

options.text: Go, but leave before the result if you get nervous
options.then: You leave early, and the clinic has to call you twice.

options.text: Put it off another month to be extra sure
options.then: One month slips into two, and the worry hangs on.

options.text: Go, and get the result that you can rely on
options.then: The counsellor goes through it with you, and the question is finally answered.

steps.why: A test taken after the window period gives you a result you can trust.

scenarios.debrief: The window period matters. Re-test to confirm.
scenarios.relearn: Test after the window period for an accurate result.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'I know my status' is a statement of strength. Feel that?
scenarios.affirm: Knowing your status is ownership and strength, never shame.
scenarios.relearn: 'I know my status' is strength and self-respect.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Anjali wants to get tested but keeps backing out, scared the result will be bad.

steps.prompt: She asks if it would be easier to just not know. What do you do?

options.text: Agree that not knowing can be easier
options.then: Anjali nods, relieved, and the test date slips away.

options.text: Tell her she's being dramatic and should just go
options.then: Anjali goes quiet. "Forget I told you."

options.text: Say knowing lets her act, and treatment works
options.then: Anjali chews her lip. "I hadn't thought of it like that."

options.text: Say she's probably fine, so there's nothing to fear
options.then: Anjali smiles, then wonders why she'd test at all if she's fine.

steps.why: Knowing lets her get care, and treatment works. That shrinks the fear.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Anjali says she's too nervous to go alone. What do you do?

options.text: Book a slot for her without asking first
options.then: Anjali feels cornered and cancels the slot.

options.text: Offer to go with her, or help her ask a trusted adult
options.then: Anjali asks her aunt to come too. Suddenly it feels doable.

options.text: Tell her she'll have to find the courage on her own
options.then: Anjali nods, and the plan quietly stalls.

options.text: Promise her the result will definitely be negative
options.then: Anjali relaxes, then worries about what happens if you're wrong.

steps.why: Company makes it easier, and a trusted adult can help her through it.

steps.prompt: Later, Anjali messages that what really scares her is a positive result. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her not to think about that at all
options.then: She tries, but lies awake thinking about nothing else.

options.text: Say that if it's positive, she can keep it secret
options.then: Anjali goes quiet. Secrecy sounds lonelier than she expected.

options.text: Say a result is information, and she won't face it alone
options.then: Anjali sends a heart. "Okay. Let's set a date this week."

options.text: Send her links about every possible infection
options.then: She reads them all and messages at 2 a.m., more scared than before.

steps.why: A result is information to act on, and support makes it easier to face.

scenarios.debrief: Fear of knowing is eased by 'you can act, and treatment works'.
scenarios.relearn: Reassure a scared friend: knowing means you can act, and treatment works.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: testing isn't a verdict on you, it's information you can use. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: A result is data to act on, never a judgement on who you are.
scenarios.relearn: A test result is information to act on, not a verdict on you.

scenarios.hook: "PrEP is only for certain people, and using it means you're promiscuous."

myth.un: PrEP is only for 'certain people' and using it means you're promiscuous.
myth.re: PrEP is a smart, judgment-free HIV-prevention tool for anyone who could benefit.
myth.why: Prevention is responsible, not a character flaw.

scenarios.relearn: PrEP is a smart prevention tool, no judgment attached.

scenarios.hook: "If you use PrEP you don't need condoms at all."

myth.un: On PrEP you don't need condoms at all.
myth.re: PrEP helps prevent HIV but not other STIs; condoms still add protection.
myth.why: Different tools cover different risks.

scenarios.relearn: PrEP prevents HIV, not other STIs; condoms still matter.

scenarios.hook: Sort: part of a complete stack, or leaves a gap?
scenarios.relearn: Combining tools and testing closes gaps; assuming or skipping leaves them.

scenarios.hook: After a health class, you decide to work out a prevention plan that fits your own life.

steps.prompt: The class listed condoms, the HPV vaccine, testing and PrEP. Where do you start?

options.text: Pick condoms only, since they're the most common
options.then: Your plan has one strong tool, with gaps the others would fill.

options.text: List which tools fit my life, and combine them
options.then: Your notes fill a page: condoms, the vaccine, regular tests, and a question about PrEP.

options.text: Copy whatever my friends say they use
options.then: Your friends' answers are mostly guesses, and none fit you exactly.

options.text: Put it off, and hope it sorts itself out
options.then: The class notes go in a drawer, and the plan waits.

steps.why: Several tools that fit your life cover more than any single one.

steps.prompt: Your friend Kabir says the vaccine and tests are overkill if you carry condoms. What do you think?

options.text: He has a point. Condoms cover most things
options.then: You settle on condoms alone, and the other tools fall away.

options.text: Each tool does a different job, so they stack
options.then: Kabir thinks. "So the vaccine covers what condoms can miss?"

options.text: Add every tool there is, whether it fits or not
options.then: The list gets long, and you doubt you'll keep up with half of it.

options.text: Condoms and tests are enough. Skip the vaccine
options.then: Kabir nods, and your plan has a gap where the vaccine would go.

steps.why: Each tool has its own job. Layering the ones you'll use closes the gaps.

steps.prompt: A month later you check how your plan is going. What do you do?

options.text: Keep what works, and see a doctor with a trusted adult
options.then: With an adult you trust beside you, a doctor helps you work out which other tools suit you.

options.text: Drop anything I haven't started yet
options.then: The plan shrinks to what was easy, and the gaps come back.

options.text: Start over with a brand-new plan from scratch
options.then: The new plan looks just like the old one, and a month is gone.

options.text: Decide the plan is fine without checking
options.then: The plan stays on paper, and you're not sure what you actually do.

steps.why: A stack you actually use, with a doctor's help on the rest, is one that protects you.

scenarios.debrief: Your stack is the tools you choose and will actually use, combined.
scenarios.relearn: Build a layered prevention stack from tools that fit your life.

scenarios.hook: A school poster mentions the HPV vaccine. You've never had it and wonder if it's worth it.

steps.prompt: Your friend Pooja says it's only for older women. What do you do?

options.text: Take her word for it and forget the poster
options.then: The poster fades into the background, and the question goes with it.

options.text: Ask a doctor whether it's right for me
options.then: The doctor says it's worth discussing, and asks you to come back with a parent.

options.text: Look it up on a forum tonight
options.then: The forum is full of opposite opinions, and you end up more confused.

options.text: Ask my older cousin what she thinks
options.then: Your cousin says she never bothered, and the question stays open.

steps.why: A doctor can tell you if the vaccine suits you. Friends and forums can only guess.

steps.prompt: A week later, the school sends a note about a vaccine camp, and your mother asks what it's for. What do you say?

options.text: It helps prevent some cancers caused by HPV
options.then: She reads the note again. "Cancer? Then let's ask the doctor together."

options.text: It's something for girls who are sexually active
options.then: Her eyebrows rise. "Why would you need that?" The talk gets tense.

options.text: No idea. It's probably not important
options.then: She puts the note aside, and the camp date passes.

options.text: Just a routine shot. Can you sign it?
options.then: She hesitates. "I'd like to know what I'm signing first."

steps.why: Naming what it prevents makes it a plain health choice your family can weigh.

steps.prompt: Pooja asks why anyone would get it before they're even dating. What do you say?

options.text: It's about health later, not who you're dating
options.then: Pooja nods. "Fair. I hadn't thought about later."

options.text: You're right. It can wait until I'm dating
options.then: Pooja nods, and the vaccine waits on a relationship.

options.text: That's none of your business, honestly
options.then: Pooja looks stung and drops it. So does the chance to share what you learned.

options.text: Everyone's getting it, so I might as well
options.then: Pooja shrugs. "Not everyone." You're not sure what to say.

steps.why: The vaccine protects your future health. It isn't tied to a relationship.

scenarios.debrief: The HPV vaccine is a powerful, lasting part of the stack.
scenarios.relearn: The HPV vaccine prevents HPV-related cancers; ask a doctor.

scenarios.hook: Things with Kunal are getting serious, and you want you both tested before sex.
scenarios.setup: You're sitting on a quiet bench after tuition.

steps.prompt: Kunal asks: "You've gone quiet. What's on your mind?"

options.text: "Nothing. Just tired from tuition."
options.then: Kunal nods. Later he spots the testing page open on your phone.

options.text: "Before we go further, can we both get tested?"
options.then: Kunal blinks, then nods slowly. "I hadn't thought of that. Why now?"

options.text: "Have you ever been tested? I'm just asking."
options.then: Kunal frowns. "Why only me? You think I've got something?"

options.text: "My friend said we should test. I don't really know."
options.then: Kunal shrugs. "If you don't know, why bother testing?"

steps.why: Asking you both to test makes it shared care, not a question about one person.

steps.prompt: Kunal says: "Isn't testing for people who've done something wrong?"

options.text: "Why? Have you done something wrong?"
options.then: Kunal's face falls. "Wow. That's what you think of me?"

options.text: "You're right. It's not really for people like us."
options.then: Kunal relaxes. "Good. So we can skip it."

options.text: "No. It's routine care, like any check-up."
options.then: Kunal thinks about it. "Huh. I never saw it like that."

options.text: "I just think it's nice to be sure, I guess."
options.then: Kunal shrugs. "Sure about what, though?"

steps.why: Testing is about health, not guilt. Saying so plainly takes the shame out of it.

steps.prompt: Next day, Kunal texts: "Thought about it. Where would we even go? I don't want people finding out."

options.text: "Let's ask your cousin. He'll know what to do."
options.then: Kunal winces. "Then my whole family knows by Sunday."

options.text: "Let's check symptoms online first and see."
options.then: You both read long lists of signs and feel no surer.

options.text: "An ICTC centre or a doctor. Both are confidential."
options.then: Kunal breathes out. "Okay. If it's private, I'm in."

options.text: "We could skip it if we're really careful."
options.then: Kunal looks relieved, and the plan to know for sure fades.

steps.why: ICTC centres and doctors test confidentially, so privacy doesn't have to stop you.

steps.prompt: Kunal asks: "If we did go, should we tell anyone?"

options.text: "No way. Nobody can ever know about this."
options.then: Kunal nods, and you both feel a little more alone with it.

options.text: "Let's tell our whole group, so it feels normal."
options.then: Kunal looks uneasy. "That's a lot of people in our business."

options.text: "Let's each think of an adult we trust to help."
options.then: Kunal thinks. "My elder sister. She'd get it."

options.text: "Only if one of the results comes back positive."
options.then: Kunal agrees, but the wait already feels heavy for you both.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help with the visit and the questions, so you don't carry it alone.

scenarios.relearn: A caring, clear 'let's both test' opens the conversation well.

scenarios.hook: You bring up protection with your partner Tanvi, and she waves it away.
scenarios.setup: You're walking home together after class.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "We don't need all that. We're fine."

options.text: "It matters to me that we both stay healthy."
options.then: Tanvi slows down. "Okay. Why does it feel so big to you?"

options.text: "I guess we'd know if something was wrong."
options.then: Tanvi nods. "Exactly. Nothing's wrong."

options.text: "If you won't talk about it, maybe we're done."
options.then: Tanvi stops walking. "Seriously? Over one comment?"

options.text: "Fine. I'll get the school nurse to explain it to you."
options.then: Tanvi rolls her eyes. "I don't need a lecture."

steps.why: Saying it matters to you keeps the talk open without blame.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "Talking about it makes it feel like we don't trust each other."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. Let's just drop it."
options.then: Tanvi smiles, relieved. The question waits for a harder moment.

options.text: "Do you have something to hide, then?"
options.then: Tanvi stares at you. "Wow. Now I'm a suspect?"

options.text: "It's not about trust. It's looking after each other."
options.then: Tanvi is quiet, then nods. "Okay. I can see that."

options.text: "I trust you. I've just read way too many health articles."
options.then: Tanvi laughs. "Stop reading them, then." The point gets lost.

steps.why: Protection is care for both of you. Naming that answers the trust worry directly.

steps.prompt: Later, Tanvi asks: "If we did plan something, what would it even be?"

options.text: "Just be careful. That's enough, right?"
options.then: Tanvi nods, but neither of you knows what careful means.

options.text: "I'll sort it out. Leave it to me."
options.then: Tanvi shrugs. "Okay." It stays your job, not a shared plan.

options.text: "Let's search it online and pick something."
options.then: You find a dozen opinions and argue about which to believe.

options.text: "Ask a doctor, maybe with an adult we trust."
options.then: Tanvi thinks. "My aunt's a nurse. She wouldn't judge."

steps.why: A doctor gives you facts that fit you, and asking together keeps it shared.

scenarios.relearn: Holding the talk kindly but firmly is reasonable and caring.

options.text: "Maybe. Let's see how things go with us first."

scenarios.hook: Your partner Aman says there's something about his health he's scared to tell you.
scenarios.setup: He keeps turning his cup round in his hands.

steps.prompt: Aman says: "I don't know how you'll take it."

options.text: "You'd better not have anything."
options.then: Aman's face shuts. After a long pause, he says it anyway, very quietly.

options.text: "Whatever it is, there's no judgement here."
options.then: Aman breathes out. "Okay. I'm going to say it straight."

options.text: "Just tell me. You're making me nervous."
options.then: Aman flinches. "Fine. I'll just say it."

options.text: "Is it bad? Just say if it's really bad."
options.then: Aman goes pale. "I knew you'd panic. Okay, here goes."

steps.why: Taking judgement off the table makes it safe for him to be honest.

steps.prompt: Aman says: "I tested positive for chlamydia. I'm on treatment now."

options.text: "Chlamydia? How did you even get that?"
options.then: Aman looks down. "Does it matter? I'm dealing with it."

options.text: "Okay. I think I need some space from you."
options.then: Aman nods stiffly. His messages go quiet for days.

options.text: "Oh no. That's so awful. Are you okay?"
options.then: Aman winces. "It's curable. Please don't make it sound like that."

options.text: "Thanks for telling me. We can handle this together."
options.then: Aman's shoulders drop. "I was so scared you'd walk away."

steps.why: Thanks and 'together' tell him honesty was safe, which is exactly what he feared.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Aman asks: "Do you think you should get tested too?"

options.text: "No need. I feel completely fine."
options.then: Aman hesitates. "Feeling fine doesn't always mean much, though."

options.text: "Yes. I'll ask Amma to help me book a doctor."
options.then: Aman nods. "Good. Tell me if you want company too."

options.text: "Only if you pay for it, since it came from you."
options.then: Aman's face drops. "Right. So it's all my fault."

options.text: "I'll just take a few of your tablets to be safe."
options.then: Aman frowns. "The doctor said they're only for me."

steps.why: Chlamydia is curable, and a test with a trusted adult's help lets you act on facts.

scenarios.relearn: A judgement-free 'we can handle it together' makes honesty safe.

scenarios.hook: "The red ribbon is about feeling sorry for sick people."

myth.un: The red ribbon is about feeling sorry for sick people.
myth.re: The red ribbon stands for solidarity and support, standing with people, not pitying them.
myth.why: Solidarity respects people as equals; pity sets them apart.

scenarios.relearn: The red ribbon means solidarity and support, not pity.

scenarios.hook: "It's fine to ask a new colleague their status before working with them."

myth.un: It's fine to ask a new colleague their status before working with them.
myth.re: Their status is private and not your business; working together carries no everyday risk.
myth.why: Demanding private health info is intrusive and based on myth.

scenarios.relearn: A colleague's status is private and not needed to work together.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: dignity means the same warm hello whether or not you know someone's status. Sit with that?
scenarios.affirm: A person's worth doesn't shift with a test result, your respect doesn't have to either.
scenarios.relearn: Someone's worth, and your respect, don't change with a result.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: if a friend ever told you their status, how would you want to show up for them?
scenarios.affirm: Any of these honours their trust, showing up steady and warm is what they'll remember.
scenarios.relearn: Honour a disclosure by listening, staying steady and offering support.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: notice the urge to gossip when you hear who got tested, what would you rather do?
scenarios.affirm: Choosing not to pass it on protects someone's privacy, that quiet choice is real dignity.
scenarios.relearn: Protecting someone's privacy is a quiet, real act of dignity.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: dignity includes how you'd talk to yourself after a hard result. What tone would you choose?
scenarios.affirm: You deserve the same kindness you'd give anyone, your worth is whole, result or not.
scenarios.relearn: Speak to yourself with the kindness you'd give a friend; your worth is whole.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a classroom where no one fears judgement is one where people actually go test. Want that?
scenarios.affirm: Every bit of judgement you drop makes it safer for someone near you to look after their health.
scenarios.relearn: Less judgement around you makes it safer for people to test.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: when you hear 'they must have done something', what's the kinder, truer thought?
scenarios.affirm: Dropping the blame story sees the human first, that's where dignity starts.
scenarios.relearn: Replace the blame story with 'anyone can be affected'.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: picture someone disclosing to you on a long bus ride home. What would you want them to feel?
scenarios.affirm: Whatever words you'd use, the feeling you give, safe and unjudged, is the heart of dignity.
scenarios.relearn: Aim to leave someone feeling safe and unjudged after they disclose.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: stigma is a habit you can unlearn, like flinching. Ready to notice yours?
scenarios.affirm: Noticing the reflex is step one, every time you choose dignity instead, the habit weakens.
scenarios.relearn: Stigma is a reflex you can notice and unlearn, one choice at a time.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: imagine your name attached to a kind, fact-based comment under a stigma post. Feel okay?
scenarios.affirm: A calm, factual voice in a noisy thread can quietly change how a whole room thinks.
scenarios.relearn: A calm, factual reply to stigma can shift a whole conversation.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: dignity for yourself means you can still dream big after a diagnosis. Believe that?
scenarios.affirm: Your studies, work and love life are still yours, a result manages, it doesn't cancel.
scenarios.relearn: A diagnosis is managed, not the end of your plans or dreams.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: who in your life would you want to feel safe enough to tell you anything about their health?
scenarios.affirm: Being that safe person is something you build, with every judgement-free reaction.
scenarios.relearn: You become a 'safe person' through judgement-free reactions.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: hostel rumour says someone went to a clinic. What's the dignified move with that rumour?
scenarios.affirm: Letting a rumour die with you is a small, powerful act of respect for someone you may not even know.
scenarios.relearn: Let a health rumour stop with you; that's respect in action.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'I know my status, and I still deserve dignity.' Can you say that for yourself?
scenarios.affirm: That sentence is yours to keep, your dignity was never up for the test in the first place.
scenarios.relearn: Your dignity isn't on the line at any test; it's always yours.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a relative jokes about a neighbour's 'illness'. What sits right for you to do?
scenarios.affirm: You don't owe a laugh to a cruel joke, even silence can refuse to feed stigma.
scenarios.relearn: You can refuse stigma simply by not laughing along.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what would a school feel like where 'get tested' was as normal as 'get your eyes checked'?
scenarios.affirm: That's the world dignity builds, where caring for your health needs no courage at all.
scenarios.relearn: Dignity makes testing as ordinary as any other health check.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: someone you admire turns out to be living with HIV. Does it change your admiration?
scenarios.affirm: Who they are didn't change with a result, and noticing that is dignity working in you.
scenarios.relearn: A status doesn't change who someone is or what they've done.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: dignity is a choice you own, no one assigns it. How do you want to spend that choice?
scenarios.affirm: Spent on respect, your choice ripples, the way you treat one person teaches everyone watching.
scenarios.relearn: Treating people with dignity is a choice you own and others learn from.

scenarios.hook: Sort: dignity for yourself, or self-stigma?
scenarios.relearn: Treatment, worth and dreams are self-dignity; 'dirty', 'deserve' and 'hide' are self-stigma.

scenarios.hook: Sort: keeps it private, or breaks confidentiality?

items.text: Telling no one without their okay
Letting them choose who to tell
Deleting a screenshot of their report

scenarios.relearn: Their consent and their choice keep it private; posting, whispering and asking around break it.

scenarios.hook: Sort: true and kind, or stigma myth?

items.text: A result is health info, not a verdict

scenarios.relearn: 'Anyone affected', 'health info' and 'treatment thrives' are true; the rest are stigma myths.

scenarios.hook: Sort: solidarity, or pity?

items.text: Talking about them sadly behind their back
Wearing the red ribbon to stand with people

scenarios.relearn: Standing with people as equals is solidarity; 'poor thing' and looking down are pity.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a calm fact about HIV, or a fear-driven myth?

items.text: Sharing a meal is completely safe
"You can catch it from a hug"

scenarios.relearn: Meals, hugs and handshakes are safe; 'catch it from a hug', mosquitoes and 'keep the cup apart' are myths.

scenarios.hook: Sort: dignity in language, or a slur?
scenarios.relearn: 'Person living with HIV' centres the person; 'the infected one' and 'diseased guy' are slurs.

scenarios.hook: Sort: dignified reaction to a disclosure, or stigma reaction?
scenarios.relearn: Thanks, sameness and support are dignity; backing away, 'don't touch' and telling others are stigma.

scenarios.hook: Sort: anti-stigma action, or stigma in disguise?

items.text: "I'm not judging, but stay away from them"
Sharing where to test, no fuss
Pretending to be kind while gossiping

scenarios.relearn: Facts, calm info and privacy fight stigma; 'not judging but...' and fake kindness hide it.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two stigma lines in this group chat.

scene.text: "Heard who went to the clinic? Spill"
"Anyone can need a test, no big deal"

scenarios.why: Demanding the gossip and 'stay away' are the stigma; the rest protect privacy and tell the truth.
scenarios.relearn: Spot stigma in 'spill the gossip' and 'stay away from him'.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two stigma lines an aunty might say.

scene.text: "Don't let your sister near that family"
"It's a health matter, not a scandal"

scenarios.why: 'Don't let her near' and 'brought shame' are the stigma; the others are fact and respect.
scenarios.relearn: Spot stigma in 'keep away from that family' and 'brought shame'.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two self-stigma thoughts to let go of.

scene.text: "I deserve to be alone for this"
"This is health info, not a verdict"

scenarios.why: 'Ruined and dirty' and 'deserve to be alone' are self-stigma; the rest are self-dignity.
scenarios.relearn: Spot self-stigma in 'I'm dirty' and 'I deserve to be alone'.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two myths about how HIV spreads.

scene.text: "You can get it from sharing a cup"

scenarios.why: Shared cups and mosquitoes are myths; the rest are true. Believing myths fuels stigma.
scenarios.relearn: Spot the myths: HIV isn't spread by shared cups or mosquitoes.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two pity lines hiding as kindness.

scene.text: "Good to see you, same as always"
"So sad, I could never cope like that"
"Tell me how I can have your back"

scenarios.why: 'Poor thing' and 'so sad' look down with pity; the rest stand beside as equals (solidarity).
scenarios.relearn: Spot pity in 'poor thing' and 'so sad'; solidarity treats people as equals.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that break confidentiality.

scene.text: "I'll just tell the warden, for safety"
"It's your news to share, not mine"
"Let me forward your report to the group"
"I won't say a word without your okay"

scenarios.why: Telling the warden and forwarding the report break confidentiality; the rest protect their choice.
scenarios.relearn: Spot the breaches: telling others or forwarding a report without consent.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two stigma lines disguised as 'just being safe'.

scene.text: "I won't share a desk with them"
"Keep their cup separate, just in case"
"Their status is private and fine by me"

scenarios.why: Refusing a desk and separating a cup are stigma dressed as caution; everyday contact is safe.
scenarios.relearn: Spot stigma-as-caution in 'won't share a desk' and 'keep their cup separate'.

scenarios.hook: At a family get-together, your cousins are laughing at a viral meme about a neighbour said to have HIV.
scenarios.setup: Your cousin Ritika holds out her phone.

steps.prompt: Ritika asks: "Have you seen this? It's Joseph uncle."

options.text: "Funny. Anyway, does anyone know when lunch is?"
options.then: Ritika laughs and passes the phone to the next cousin.

options.text: "That's a real person's health. I'm not into that."
options.then: Ritika's smile slips. "It's just a meme." She lowers the phone.

options.text: "You're all so cruel. Honestly, grow up."
options.then: The cousins roll their eyes. Ritika keeps reading the comments aloud.

options.text: "Ha. Send it to me. My friends will love it."
options.then: She forwards it, and now it sits in your phone too.

steps.why: Saying it plainly reminds them a real person is being laughed at.

steps.prompt: Your cousin Dev says: "Everyone says he got it from bad habits anyway."

options.text: "Maybe, but it's still mean to laugh."
options.then: Dev nods. "See? Even you agree."

options.text: "Nobody gets HIV for being bad. It's a virus."
options.then: Dev shrugs. "Okay. I didn't think of it like that."

options.text: "Who says that? Which aunty?"
options.then: Dev names three people, and the story grows in the telling.

options.text: "I don't know anything about his habits."
options.then: Dev takes that as a maybe, and keeps talking.

steps.why: HIV is a virus, never a punishment. Saying so stops the blame story.

steps.prompt: Later, your aunt says: "Don't go near Joseph uncle's house, beta."

options.text: "Okay, Aunty. You know best about these things."
options.then: She nods, satisfied. The meme and the warning travel on together.

options.text: "That's so ignorant, Aunty."
options.then: Your aunt's face hardens. "Don't talk to me like that."

options.text: "It doesn't spread by visiting, Aunty. He's our neighbour."
options.then: Your aunt pauses. "Really?" She looks less sure.

options.text: "Don't worry, Aunty. I wasn't planning to go there anyway."
options.then: Your aunt smiles. Joseph uncle's gate stays closed to your family.

steps.why: A calm fact, said respectfully, can shift an elder's fear.

scenarios.relearn: Name it: a real person's health isn't meme material.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Pooja has just told you her test came back positive.
scenarios.setup: She goes quiet, watching your face.

steps.prompt: Pooja says softly: "Say something. Please."

options.text: "Oh... um, okay."
options.then: Pooja looks away. "Forget I said anything."

options.text: "What were you thinking? You should've been careful."
options.then: Pooja flinches. "I knew you'd say that."

options.text: "Thank you for telling me. I'm here. Nothing changes."
options.then: Pooja's eyes fill. "I was so scared you'd see me differently."

options.text: "Oh no, you poor thing. This is awful."
options.then: Pooja's face crumples. "So it is as bad as I thought."

steps.why: Thanks and 'nothing changes' answer the fear she had in telling you.

steps.prompt: Pooja asks: "Do you think I'll be okay?"

options.text: "Of course. It's probably nothing."
options.then: Pooja frowns. "It's not nothing. It's positive."

options.text: "Treatment works. Do you have a doctor to ask?"
options.then: "The clinic counsellor," she says. "I go back on Monday."

options.text: "I don't know. It depends what it is."
options.then: Pooja's worry deepens. She starts imagining the worst.

options.text: "Let me look it all up online for you right now."
options.then: The first search results scare you both more than they help.

steps.why: Treatment works, and her doctor is the right person for the medical answers.

steps.prompt: Pooja says: "I can't tell my parents. Promise you won't either."

options.text: "I promise. Nobody ever needs to know."
options.then: Pooja nods, relieved, and plans to handle it all alone.

options.text: "You have to tell them. They're your parents."
options.then: Pooja shakes her head. "You don't know my parents."

options.text: "It's yours to tell. Is there an adult you'd trust?"
options.then: Pooja thinks. "Maybe my Maasi. She'd know what to do."

options.text: "I think I should tell them for you."
options.then: Pooja panics. "No! I trusted you."

steps.why: Her news is hers to share, and finding a trusted adult means she isn't alone.

steps.prompt: A week later, Pooja says: "I feel like everyone can tell just by looking at me."

options.text: "Maybe stay home for a bit till you feel better."
options.then: Pooja stays in for days, and feels more alone, not less.

options.text: "Just act normal and nobody will suspect."
options.then: Pooja stiffens. "Suspect what? That something's wrong with me?"

options.text: "No one can tell by looking. You're still you."
options.then: Pooja laughs a little. "Still me. Okay."

options.text: "Honestly, people are too busy to notice."
options.then: Pooja nods, but she doesn't look convinced.

steps.why: Nobody can see status. Hearing she's still herself eases the fear of being seen.

scenarios.relearn: Meet a disclosure with warmth and 'nothing changes between us'.

scenarios.hook: Your classmate Siddharth has a screenshot of another student's leaked test report.
scenarios.setup: His thumb hovers over the hostel group.

steps.prompt: Siddharth asks: "Should I post it? Everyone will want to see."

options.text: "Eh, everyone'll find out anyway."
options.then: He shrugs and hits send. Phones start buzzing down the corridor.

options.text: "Up to you. I'm staying out of it."
options.then: Siddharth takes that as a yes and starts typing a caption.

options.text: "Blur the name first, then it's fine."
options.then: "They'll guess anyway," he says, and blurs it badly.

options.text: "No. That's private, and it would really hurt him."
options.then: Siddharth hesitates, his thumb still over the screen.

steps.why: A clear no, with the reason, gives him a reason to stop.

steps.prompt: Siddharth says: "Honestly, people have a right to know who's positive."

options.text: "Fair, but maybe wait until it's confirmed."
options.then: "So you agree," he says, and goes looking for the source.

options.text: "Nobody has a right to someone's health info."
options.then: Siddharth frowns. "I guess I wouldn't want mine out there."

options.text: "Whatever. I don't want to argue about it."
options.then: He takes that as agreement and keeps scrolling.

options.text: "You'd be the first to cry if it was yours."
options.then: Siddharth bristles. "That's not the point."

steps.why: Health information belongs to the person, and nobody else gets to share it.

steps.prompt: Siddharth asks: "So what do I do with the screenshot now?"

options.text: "Keep it, but don't show anyone."
options.then: The screenshot sits in his phone, one tap from being shared.

options.text: "Send it to him so he knows it's out."
options.then: Seeing his own report on someone else's phone, the classmate goes pale.

options.text: "Delete it, and ask whoever sent it to delete it."
options.then: He deletes it, then messages the sender: "Bin it, man."

options.text: "Forward it to the warden as proof."
options.then: Now the warden has a copy too, and one more person has seen it.

steps.why: Deleting it, and asking the sender to delete it too, stops the leak spreading.

steps.prompt: Next morning, Siddharth says: "It's still going round other groups."

options.text: "Let's find out who leaked it and expose them."
options.then: The hunt becomes its own rumour, with the classmate's name at its centre.

options.text: "Nothing we can do now. It's out."
options.then: By lunch, the report has reached two more hostels.

options.text: "Let's post in every group that it's fake."
options.then: Calling it fake only draws more people to go and look.

options.text: "Let's get the warden to step in."
options.then: The warden thanks you and says she'll deal with it quietly.

steps.why: A trusted adult can stop a leak, and nobody needs to share it again to report it.

scenarios.relearn: Refuse to forward a private report; protect their confidentiality.

scenarios.hook: Planning Diwali lunch, your uncle wants to leave out Shalini Aunty because she has HIV.
scenarios.setup: Everyone at the table goes quiet.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "People with HIV shouldn't eat with everyone. It isn't safe."

options.text: "Maybe she could have a separate plate, to be safe."
options.then: Your uncle nods. "Good thinking." A separate plate becomes the plan.

options.text: "Let's not argue about this today, please."
options.then: Your mother cuts in before he decides: "Let's hear this out."

options.text: "That's a disgusting thing to say."
options.then: Your uncle's face reddens. "Don't speak to me like that."

options.text: "It doesn't spread through food or sitting together."
options.then: Your uncle frowns. "Are you sure? That's not what I heard."

steps.why: A calm fact answers the fear, which is what is really behind his worry.

steps.prompt: Your uncle asks the table: "And if she uses our glasses and the water jug?"

options.text: "Maybe keep her things separate, just to be sure."
options.then: Your uncle nods. A separate steel glass is set aside for her.

options.text: "That's safe too. Everyday things don't pass it on."
options.then: Your uncle rubs his chin. "Hm. Your aunt said the same."

options.text: "I'm not sure about that one, honestly."
options.then: Your uncle takes the doubt as proof. "See? Nobody knows."

options.text: "Just look it up before you say such things."
options.then: Your uncle bristles. "Don't lecture me in front of everyone."

steps.why: Everyday sharing carries no risk. Saying so plainly clears up the fear.

steps.prompt: Your grandmother says quietly: "But what will people say if she comes?"

options.text: "Who cares what people say?"
options.then: Dadi looks hurt. "I care. I have to live here."

options.text: "Maybe she could come, but leave early."
options.then: Dadi nods. Shalini Aunty is invited, but only for the start.

options.text: "They'll see a family that treats her with respect."
options.then: Dadi is quiet, then nods. "She has always been good to us."

options.text: "You're right, Dadi. Maybe she should skip this year."
options.then: Dadi sighs with relief, and Shalini Aunty is left off the list.

steps.why: Including her fully is what dignity looks like, and it shows others how.

scenarios.relearn: Calmly correct the myth: HIV isn't spread by sharing meals.

scenarios.hook: In biology class, the teacher steps out and the talk turns to STIs.
scenarios.setup: Your classmate Varun raises his voice so everyone hears.

steps.prompt: Varun says: "Only certain types of people get those infections, obviously."

options.text: "Ha. Yeah, obviously. Everyone knows that."
options.then: Varun grins. "See? Everyone knows." A few people laugh.

options.text: "Which types? Go on, name them."
options.then: Varun starts listing groups, and the class laughs at each one.

options.text: "Anyone can get them. It's health, not types."
options.then: A few people nod. Varun shrugs. "I'm just saying."

options.text: "Wow, so ignorant. Typical Varun."
options.then: Varun's ears go red, and he doubles down, louder.

steps.why: Anyone can be affected. Saying so takes the stereotype apart without a fight.

steps.prompt: Varun says: "Nobody ever admits to having one. Doesn't that say something?"

options.text: "Yeah. It says it's embarrassing to have one."
options.then: Varun smirks. "Exactly my point."

options.text: "It says shame like this stops people testing."
options.then: Varun goes quiet. Someone at the back says, "Fair."

options.text: "I don't know. Let's just leave it."
options.then: Varun takes that as a win and carries on joking.

options.text: "It says people like you make everything a joke."
options.then: The class goes "ooh". Varun scowls, and it turns personal.

steps.why: Stigma makes people hide and skip tests. Naming that shows the real harm.

steps.prompt: After class, Varun asks quietly: "Who's actually meant to get tested, anyway?"

options.text: "Only people who've done something risky."
options.then: Varun nods. "So not for people like us, then."

options.text: "Why, are you worried about something?"
options.then: Varun goes red. "No! Forget I asked."

options.text: "Look it up. I'm done talking about this."
options.then: Varun shrugs and never does.

options.text: "Anyone who's sexually active. It's routine."
options.then: Varun nods. "Huh. Nobody ever said it like that."

steps.why: Testing is about behaviour, not types of people. Anyone who needs it can use it.

scenarios.relearn: Name it: infection is about health, not a 'type' of person.

scenarios.hook: After a positive result, you're alone in your room, replaying everything.
scenarios.setup: You catch your own eyes in the mirror.

steps.prompt: A harsh voice in your head says: "You really messed everything up."

options.text: "Yeah. I did this to myself."
options.then: The voice gets louder. "And everyone will know it."

options.text: "This is health info, not a verdict on me."
options.then: The voice falters. Your breathing slows a little.

options.text: "I just need to stop thinking about it."
options.then: The thought pushes back harder the more you push it away.

options.text: "Others have it worse, so I shouldn't feel this."
options.then: The voice goes quiet, but the hurt underneath stays.

steps.why: A result is information, never a verdict on who you are.

steps.prompt: The voice says: "You can't tell anyone. They'll think less of you."

options.text: "True. I'll keep this to myself forever."
options.then: The room feels smaller, and the secret heavier.

options.text: "I'll tell someone once I've sorted it all out."
options.then: Sorting it alone feels endless, and the evening drags on.

options.text: "The right people won't. I can pick who to tell."
options.then: The thought loosens. Your aunt Rekha's face comes to mind.

options.text: "Maybe I should pretend it never happened."
options.then: For a moment it's easier. Then you remember your follow-up date.

steps.why: Choosing someone you trust means you don't have to carry this alone.

steps.prompt: Next day, the clinic counsellor asks: "How are you feeling about the result?"

options.text: "Fine. I just want to get it sorted."
options.then: She nods, but notices your hands shaking.

options.text: "I deserve it, really."
options.then: She leans in. "Nobody deserves an infection. Can we talk about that?"

options.text: "Honestly, ashamed. Can we talk about that?"
options.then: "Of course," she says. "Shame is common. It's not the truth about you."

options.text: "I'd rather not talk about feelings."
options.then: She nods and moves on. The heaviness comes home with you.

steps.why: Honesty with a counsellor gets you real support. You deserve care, not shame.

scenarios.relearn: Speak to yourself with dignity: it's health info, not a verdict.

scenarios.hook: Manav, a senior, heard you were at the ICTC centre and wants to know who else was there.
scenarios.setup: He catches you by the bike stand.

steps.prompt: Manav says: "Come on. Who did you see there? I won't tell."

options.text: "I didn't see anyone I knew."
options.then: Manav narrows his eyes. "Really? Someone said otherwise."

options.text: "Tell me why first, and I'll think about it."
options.then: Manav grins. "Now we're talking."

options.text: "That's not mine to share, or yours either."
options.then: Manav smirks. "So you did see someone."

options.text: "Why do you even care who was there?"
options.then: "Just curious," Manav shrugs. "Everyone wants to know."

steps.why: A plain 'not mine to share' protects them without lies or bargaining.

steps.prompt: Manav says: "Everyone who goes there is sick. So who was it?"

options.text: "I went for a friend, not for me."
options.then: Manav smirks. "Sure you did." Now he's curious about you too.

options.text: "People go there for routine tests. I'm still not saying."
options.then: Manav rolls his eyes, but he's run out of angles.

options.text: "Yeah, probably. But I still won't say."
options.then: Manav nods. "Knew it. So someone there is sick."

options.text: "Why? Are you sick or something?"
options.then: Manav's face darkens, and the talk turns uglier.

steps.why: Correcting the myth, and still keeping quiet about names, protects everyone who tests.

steps.prompt: Later, your best friend Ira asks: "Just tell me who. I won't tell Manav."

options.text: "Okay, just you. Promise you won't tell?"
options.then: Ira promises. By Friday, Manav knows the name anyway.

options.text: "I'll give you a hint. They're in our class."
options.then: Ira starts guessing out loud, name by name.

options.text: "Not even you. It isn't mine to tell."
options.then: Ira huffs, then laughs. "Fine. You're annoyingly loyal."

options.text: "Why does everyone care so much?"
options.then: Ira shrugs. "Because it's juicy." She keeps asking.

steps.why: A confidence holds only if it holds with everyone, even close friends.

steps.prompt: Your classmate Neha, who you saw there, says quietly: "Manav keeps looking at me. Has he been asking?"

options.text: "Don't worry. He's just being nosy about everyone."
options.then: Neha nods, unsure, and Manav keeps watching her.

options.text: "He has. I won't help him, and if he keeps on, I'll tell a teacher."
options.then: Neha breathes out. "Thank you. I was so worried."

options.text: "He has. But why were you there, anyway?"
options.then: Neha's face closes. "Does it matter?"

options.text: "He has, so be careful. Maybe skip the bike stand."
options.then: Neha nods and starts taking the long way round, alone with it.

steps.why: Keeping her privacy, with a teacher to turn to if Manav persists, protects her.

scenarios.relearn: Refuse to out who you saw testing; their privacy isn't yours to share.

scenarios.hook: Aman, who you've been dating for two months, tells you he is living with HIV.

steps.prompt: Days later, a friend asks why you and Aman both seemed so serious. What do you say?

options.then: Your friend teases you a little, then moves on. Aman's news stays his.

options.text: Keep it from him so he doesn't get upset

options.text: Tell him, and ask what he'd like you to do

scenarios.hook: "If I feel fine, I don't need a test."

myth.un: Feeling fine means I don't need a test.
myth.re: Many STIs cause no symptoms at all; feeling well tells you nothing.
myth.why: Only a test, not how you feel, can tell you your status.

scenarios.relearn: Feeling fine proves nothing; only a test tells you your status.

scenarios.hook: "Asking where to test is embarrassing."

myth.un: Asking where to test is embarrassing.
myth.re: Clinic staff handle these questions every day; it's a normal health request.
myth.why: Walking in informed is self-respect, not something to blush about.

scenarios.relearn: Asking to test is a normal health request, not something to be shy about.

scenarios.hook: "A negative result means I'm covered for life."

myth.un: One negative result covers me for life.
myth.re: Status can change with new exposures; testing fits your situation over time.
myth.why: A result reflects a moment, so testing stays part of ongoing self-care.

scenarios.relearn: A negative result is a snapshot; keep testing as your life changes.

scenarios.hook: "Testing positive ends your life."

myth.un: Testing positive ends your life.
myth.re: Treatment works; people who know their status live full, healthy lives.
myth.why: Knowing early opens the door to care, the opposite of an ending.

scenarios.relearn: A result is a starting point for care, never the end of a life.

scenarios.hook: "Only people with many partners need testing."

myth.un: Only people with many partners need testing.
myth.re: Anyone sexually active can benefit; it takes only one exposure.
myth.why: Testing is about behaviour and care, never a count or a label.

scenarios.relearn: Testing is for anyone active, not a judgement on how many partners.

scenarios.hook: "A clinic will tell my parents or college."

myth.un: A clinic will tell my parents or college.
myth.re: Confidential services keep your visit private; that's part of the care.
myth.why: Privacy is built in so you can seek help without fear.

scenarios.relearn: Confidential testing keeps your visit private; privacy is built in.

scenarios.hook: "A self-test result can't be trusted at all."

myth.un: A self-test result can't be trusted.
myth.re: Used correctly and read after the window period, self-tests are reliable.
myth.why: They're a valid, private way to learn your status at home.

scenarios.relearn: Self-tests are reliable when used right and read after the window period.

scenarios.hook: "Getting tested invites bad luck."

myth.un: Getting tested invites bad luck.
myth.re: A test changes nothing about your body; it only gives you the facts.
myth.why: Knowledge lets you act early, which is the opposite of harm.

scenarios.relearn: A test only reveals facts; it can't cause anything.

scenarios.hook: "I should wait until I have symptoms to test."

myth.un: I should wait for symptoms before testing.
myth.re: Most infections stay silent, so waiting for symptoms misses them.
myth.why: Routine testing, not symptom-watching, is how you stay informed.

scenarios.relearn: Don't wait for symptoms; most infections are silent, so test routinely.

scenarios.hook: "If a partner looks clean, no test is needed."

myth.un: If a partner looks clean, no test is needed.
myth.re: You can't see status; healthy-looking people can carry an STI unknowingly.
myth.why: Only testing, never appearance, tells either of you the facts.

scenarios.relearn: Looks reveal nothing; only a test tells you or a partner your status.

scenarios.hook: "Testing is only an HIV thing."

myth.un: Testing is only about HIV.
myth.re: A check can cover several STIs, many curable, not HIV alone.
myth.why: Knowing your full status lets you act on whatever shows up.

scenarios.relearn: Testing can cover several STIs, many curable, not just HIV.

scenarios.hook: "Knowing my status changes who I am."

myth.un: Knowing my status changes who I am.
myth.re: A result is health information, never a statement about your character.
myth.why: You're the same person; now you have facts you can act on.

scenarios.relearn: A result is health information, not a statement about who you are.

scenarios.hook: "There's no point testing if I can't afford treatment."

myth.un: No point testing if I can't afford treatment.
myth.re: Public services offer free testing and care; cost shouldn't stop you.
myth.why: Knowing early connects you to support that's actually within reach.

scenarios.relearn: Free public testing and care exist, so cost shouldn't stop you knowing.

options.text: Trust yourself to remember without any help
options.then: You don't, and another season passes.

options.text: Go only when a friend happens to remind you
options.then: Nobody reminds you.

options.text: Set a repeating reminder on your phone
options.then: Your phone pings on the date. Booking takes two minutes.

options.text: Wait for a scare to push you into it
options.then: Scares don't come on a schedule, and neither does testing.

steps.why: A repeating reminder makes testing routine, so it no longer depends on memory.

scenarios.debrief: Treat testing like any health appointment, scheduled and done.
scenarios.relearn: Schedule testing like any appointment so it actually happens.

scenarios.hook: At a clinic for an HIV test, the doctor offers to check for other STIs too.

steps.prompt: She says it can all be done in the same visit. What do you do?

options.text: Refuse everything except the HIV test
options.then: The doctor writes up only the HIV test, and the rest stays unchecked.

options.text: Accept, so you know your whole status
options.then: The doctor nods and adds a few tests to the form.

options.text: Accept only the tests that sound least awkward
options.then: You pick by name, not by what matters, and leave gaps.

options.text: Ask to do the others another day
options.then: "Another day" joins your list of good intentions.

steps.why: Many STIs have no signs, and several are curable, so knowing more helps.

steps.prompt: Before the test, the doctor asks a few questions about your health. What do you do?

options.text: Give short answers to get it over with
options.then: She has to guess, and some questions go unasked.

options.text: Ask why she needs to know, sounding annoyed
options.then: She explains patiently, but the visit gets tense.

options.text: Say what you think she'd like to hear
options.then: Her advice rests on answers that aren't quite true.

options.text: Answer honestly, since it's confidential
options.then: She listens without a flicker and notes what matters.

steps.why: Honest answers help the doctor give the right care, and she treats them with respect and privacy.

steps.prompt: A friend says only HIV tests matter, since other STIs aren't serious. What do you say?

options.text: Agree, since HIV is the only one people talk about
options.then: Your friend nods, and plans to skip the rest next time.

options.text: Say other STIs are worse than HIV
options.then: Your friend looks scared now, and less likely to test at all.

options.text: Say other STIs matter too, and most are treatable
options.then: Your friend thinks. "So it's worth checking for all of them?"

options.text: Say you don't know enough to say
options.then: Your friend takes that as agreement.

steps.why: Most STIs are treatable, and finding them early is why a fuller check helps.

scenarios.debrief: A fuller check tells you your whole status, and several STIs are curable.
scenarios.relearn: A fuller STI check is worth it; most STIs are treatable, several curable.

scenarios.hook: None of your friends mention testing, and you feel like the only one who thinks about it.

steps.prompt: You're thinking of booking your first test. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since none of your friends are testing
options.then: You fit in, and the question stays open.

options.text: Wait until it feels more normal among your friends
options.then: Months pass, and nobody brings it up.

options.text: Book it, but only if a friend agrees to test too
options.then: Your friend laughs it off, and your plan goes with it.

options.text: Book it anyway, as a way of respecting yourself
options.then: You book a slot for Saturday. It feels like your own decision.

steps.why: Your health is yours. Testing is self-respect, with or without company.

steps.prompt: Your friend Kabir jokes that only people with something to hide get tested. What do you do?

options.text: Laugh along so you don't stand out from the group
options.then: Kabir moves on, and testing feels a bit further away.

options.text: Say testing is self-care, like any check-up
options.then: Kabir pauses. "Huh. Never thought of it like that."

options.text: Say you'd never get tested yourself
options.then: Kabir nods. Now testing feels like something to hide.

options.text: Tell him he's ignorant and storm off
options.then: Kabir rolls his eyes, and the myth goes unchallenged.

steps.why: Testing is routine self-care, not a sign of anything to hide.

steps.prompt: A month later, Kabir quietly asks where someone could get tested. What do you do?

options.text: Tease him about his earlier joke
options.then: Kabir goes red and drops the question.

options.text: Ask him what he's done to need one
options.then: Kabir shuts down. "Forget it."

options.text: Tell him where to go, and that it's confidential
options.then: Kabir saves the address. "Thanks. Keep this between us?"

options.text: Say he should ask someone who knows more than you
options.then: Kabir never asks anyone else.

steps.why: Sharing the facts kindly makes testing normal, one person at a time.

scenarios.debrief: Testing is self-respect. You don't need permission or company.
scenarios.relearn: Testing is self-respect; you don't need anyone's company to do it.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what makes a test feel like care rather than a chore?
scenarios.affirm: For future you, for a partner, one small step, all of it is care.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: if a friend told you they got tested, what would you feel?
scenarios.affirm: Respect and gladness, exactly the response testing deserves.
scenarios.relearn: Testing earns respect; that's the response it deserves.

scenarios.affirm: Calm, nervous or ready, every honest feeling is okay; you can still go.

scenarios.affirm: Taking charge, brave or just normal, however you frame it, it's yours.
scenarios.relearn: However you frame it, testing is you taking charge of your health.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that are myths, not testing facts.

scene.text: "Only a test can tell you your status"
"You can tell an STI by looking"

scenarios.why: You can't see status, and feeling well proves nothing; only a test tells you.
scenarios.relearn: Looks and feeling well prove nothing; only a test tells you your status.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two shame lines hiding among the supportive ones.

scene.text: "If you test, you must have done wrong"
"A result is information, not a verdict"

scenarios.why: 'Dirty' and 'you must have done wrong' are shame; the rest are the truth.
scenarios.relearn: Reject shame lines like 'dirty' and 'you did wrong'; testing is self-care.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two bad reasons to skip a test.

scene.text: "My partner looks healthy, so we're fine"
"I've waited out the window, time to test"

scenarios.why: Looks tell you nothing and luck isn't real; both are weak reasons to skip.
scenarios.relearn: 'They look healthy' and 'it'll jinx me' are not reasons to skip a test.

"I'll tell people on my own terms"
"I shared her result in our group chat"
"My status is mine to share or not"

scenarios.why: Naming who you saw and sharing her result both break confidentiality.
scenarios.relearn: Outing who tested or sharing a result breaks confidentiality; status is private.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two false claims about test results.

scene.text: "A positive result is information to act on"
"A positive result means nothing can be done"

scenarios.why: 'Nothing can be done' and 'covered forever' are both false; act and re-test.
scenarios.relearn: 'Nothing can be done' and 'covered forever' are false; treatment works, re-test.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two myths about where and how to test.

scene.text: "NACO ICTC testing is free and confidential"
"Clinics will report you to your college"
"You need lots of money to get tested"
"A doctor you trust is a real route"
